newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian central bank brakes rupee's rise vs dollar.
newsitem.headline: Indian central bank brakes rupee's rise vs dollar.

text.p: The Indian rupee softened on Friday after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened to cap the currency's gains but it remained around its strongest level for seven months against the U.S. dollar, dealers said.
They said the RBI bought dollars after the rupee broke through the 35.70 per dollar barrier, pushing the rupee down to 35.725 in afternoon trade.
"The whole purpose of today's trade was to find at what level the RBI will show its hand," said Ravi Kumar, chief forex dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank.
"It was a classic market versus RBI situation. And show their hands they did."
But the rupee recovered once the RBI went off the market to end at 35.71/72 against its previous close of 35.735/745.
Dealers said Friday's trade was crucial in determining whether the RBI was prepared to defend the dollar.

Lack of central bank intervention was largely responsible for the rupee hitting a seven-month high on Thursday, dealers said. Opening at 35.755/765, the rupee hit an intraday high of 35.735 as the RBI kept to the sidelines.
The RBI's absence from the market on Thursday triggered speculation on whether the central bank would check the rupee's gains or let market forces determine the exchange rate.

Dealers said the RBI has been constrained by the impact intervention has on the domestic money market. The RBI's dollar purchases cause an injection of rupees into the banking system, boosting money supply growth.
The latest RBI data shows 16.6 percent year-on-year growth in the M3 measure of money supply for the two weeks ended June 6. It has set a target of 15.0-15.5 percent for 1997/98 (April-March).
The Business Standard daily said on Friday that the RBI had decided not to intervene unless there was an "extreme provocation."
The decision was made after a meeting between RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan and finance minister P. Chidambaram last Saturday, the newspaper said.
An RBI spokeswoman declined to comment on the report.
The spokeswoman said RBI's intervention policy was guided by the demand-supply situation in the market and it sought to even out any mismatches.
The other objective was to keep the value of the rupee close to the real effective exchange rate, the spokeswoman added.
Indian exporters have recently complained about the exchange rate, saying the rupee was overvalued and its strength had hurt their competitiveness in international markets.
On Friday, neighbouring Pakistan devalued its currency and dealers said the move was a technical correction to adjust for the U.S. dollar's appreciation against major currencies.

The rupee has been buoyant for the past year due to healthy currency inflows and poor demand for the U.S. dollar. Inflows have been mainly from foreign investment and foreign currency borrowings by Indian corporates.
India's foreign currency reserves leapt to $25.4 billion on June 27 from $19.7 billion on February 28.
